pos: n. phr. (the breath God breathed into man, and the life-principle of all living creatures)
etymology: Hebrew nishmath chayyim in Genesis 2:7, from neshamah, breath or spirit, and chayyim, lives; and ruach chayyim in Genesis 6:17, from ruach, wind, breath, or spirit.
biblical_def: The phrase enters Scripture at the making of man: “And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.” Two actions are distinguished and both are necessary. The forming is of dust, which man shares with the beasts and the ground he was taken from; the breathing is direct, personal, and into the nostrils, and it is what makes the formed dust a living soul. The Authorized Version uses the same English phrase for the wider animal creation in the flood narrative — God destroys “all flesh, wherein is the breath of life”, and “All in whose nostrils was the breath of life, of all that was in the dry land, died” — so that the phrase names the life-principle of every breathing creature. The distinctive thing about man is not therefore that he breathes but the manner of his receiving: of no beast is it said that God breathed into his nostrils. Elihu states the doctrine plainly: “The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life.” The breath is given and is not owned. Scripture presses this: God “takest away their breath, they die, and return to their dust”, which means that every creature's continuance is a moment-by-moment loan. Life is not a possession secured at the beginning but a gift sustained, and it returns when He recalls it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Breath, the air inhaled and expelled in respiration; life. The breath of life, Genesis 2:7, that which God breathed into man's nostrils, whereby he became a living soul.
webster_full: Breath, the air inhaled and expelled in the respiration of animals.
Life; the power of breathing, and therefore of living.
Hebrew neshamah, breath, used of the breath God breathed into man.
Hebrew ruach, wind, breath, spirit, used of the breath of life in all flesh.
God breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, Genesis 2:7.
scriptures: Gen 2:7
And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
Gen 6:17
And, behold, I, even I, do bring a flood of waters upon the earth, to destroy all flesh, wherein is the breath of life, from under heaven; and every thing that is in the earth shall die.
Gen 7:22
All in whose nostrils was the breath of life, of all that was in the dry land, died.
Job 33:4
The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life.
corruption_summary: Life is reduced to a chemical process that arose without a giver, and the breathing into the nostrils — the ground of human dignity and of the body's goodness — is lost with it.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern materialism holds that life is an arrangement of matter arrived at without intention, so that the difference between a living man and a dead one is a difference of chemistry and nothing further. Everything in Genesis 2:7 contradicts this, and the consequences are not abstract. If the breath is not given, it is not owed back, and no account can be given of why a life should be held sacred rather than useful. The doctrine that God breathed into man's nostrils is the foundation under the prohibition of murder in Genesis 9:6, and a culture that has let go of the former will not long keep the latter. Scripture's claim is that the breath in every man is on loan from the God who takes it away and who will require it.

A second and opposite error is older and runs through much popular Christian speech: the body is treated as a container and the real man as the breath inside it, so that salvation becomes escape from the flesh and the resurrection of the body is quietly dropped. Genesis will not have this either. Man does not receive a soul and keep it in a body; the formed dust plus the breathed breath becomes a living soul, and the whole man is what is meant. This is why the Christian hope is resurrection and not the immortality of a disembodied spirit, and why the body is called the temple of the Holy Ghost. The principle to recover is the unity of the man God made: dust that God breathed into, honourable in both halves, and owing every breath to the One who gave it.
roots_summary: Hebrew neshamah, breath; ruach, wind, breath, spirit; chayyim, lives; the life-principle given by God and recalled by Him.

pos: n. phr. (the material from which man was formed, and to which he returns)
etymology: Hebrew aphar min ha-adamah — aphar, dust or dry earth, and adamah, ground or soil, the word from which Adam is drawn. The man is named for the ground he was taken from.
biblical_def: “And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.” The Hebrew carries a wordplay the English cannot: adam, the man, is formed from adamah, the ground, so that his name is the name of the soil. The verb formed is the potter's word, and the picture is deliberate — God does not command man into being from a distance as He commands the light, but stoops and works the clay. The phrase returns as a sentence after the fall: “for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.” Death in Scripture is therefore not annihilation but a reversal of the forming, the undoing of Genesis 2:7 in both of its parts — the breath withdrawn and the dust returned. The Preacher states the universality without comfort: “All go unto one place; all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again.” Two doctrines sit in this phrase, and Scripture holds them together without embarrassment. Man is dust, which is the ground of a real humility, and Abraham uses it exactly so when he approaches God as one “which am but dust and ashes.” And man is dust that God personally formed and breathed into, which is the ground of a real dignity. Neither cancels the other.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Dust, fine dry particles of earth; also, the earth as the receptacle of the dead; and figuratively, a low or mean condition. The dust of the ground, Genesis 2:7, the material of which man was formed.
webster_full: Dust, fine, dry particles of earth or other matter.
The grave; the earth as the receptacle of the dead.
Hebrew aphar, dust, dry earth, rubbish.
Hebrew adamah, ground or soil, whence the name Adam.
Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return, Genesis 3:19.
scriptures: Gen 2:7
And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
Gen 3:19
In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.
Ecc 3:20
All go unto one place; all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again.
And Abraham answered and said, Behold now, I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord, which am but dust and ashes:
corruption_summary: The phrase is used to prove man is nothing but matter, or else embarrassedly explained away, when Scripture holds the dust and the divine forming together as humility and dignity at once.
corruption_paragraphs: The reductive reading takes dust as the whole account: man is chemistry, his sense of significance an evolutionary artefact, his death simply the dispersal of material. The verse says nothing of the kind, and its grammar refuses it. The dust is what God formed, with the potter's verb, and into which He breathed. To quote the first half against the second is not to read Genesis but to edit it. The practical cost is visible wherever human beings are valued by their usefulness, since dust that no one formed has no claim on anyone's mercy.

The opposite embarrassment is found inside the church, where the dust is softened because it sounds demeaning. It is not demeaning; it is load-bearing. The dust is what makes grace grace, and Scripture's great prayers lean on it — Abraham pleading as dust and ashes, the psalmist remembering that God knows our frame. It is also the ground of the Christian's hope rather than an obstacle to it, since the God who formed dust the first time is not short of power to raise it, and the resurrection of the body is the redemption of this material and not an escape from it. The principle to recover is that both halves of Genesis 2:7 must be preached: man is dust, and so has nothing to boast of; man is dust God breathed into, and so is never disposable.

pos: n. phr. (the openings of the sky, used of the flood and of overwhelming blessing)
etymology: Hebrew arubboth ha-shamayim — arubbah, a lattice, sluice, or window, from a root meaning to lie in wait or to be latticed; and shamayim, the heavens.
biblical_def: The phrase is used in Scripture of judgment and of blessing, and the same figure serves both. At the flood: “the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened,” and when the judgment is finished, “The fountains also of the deep and the windows of heaven were stopped, and the rain from heaven was restrained.” The imagery is of latticed openings in the sky that God unbars and bars again, and the pairing with the fountains of the deep means the flood came from above and below at once — a deliberate undoing of the second day's separation of the waters. Malachi turns the same figure to mercy in the one passage where God invites His people to test Him: “Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse… and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.” A third occurrence is a warning about unbelief. When Elisha promised plenty in a besieged and starving Samaria, a lord on whose hand the king leaned answered, “Behold, if the LORD would make windows in heaven, might this thing be?” The prophet's reply is exact: “thou shalt see it with thine eyes, but shalt not eat thereof.” The man used the figure to mock a promise, and was granted the sight and denied the supper.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Window, an opening in a wall for the admission of light. The windows of heaven, Genesis 7:11, the openings of the sky, used both of the flood and of overflowing blessing.
webster_full: Window, an opening in the wall of a building for the admission of light.
Hebrew arubbah, a lattice, a sluice, a window or opening.
The windows of heaven were opened, Genesis 7:11, at the flood.
The windows of heaven were stopped, Genesis 8:2, when it was stayed.
Open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, Malachi 3:10.
scriptures: Gen 7:11

In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, the seventeenth day of the month, the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened.
Gen 8:2
The fountains also of the deep and the windows of heaven were stopped, and the rain from heaven was restrained;
Mal 3:10

Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.

Then a lord on whose hand the king leaned answered the man of God, and said, Behold, if the LORD would make windows in heaven, might this thing be? And he said, Behold, thou shalt see it with thine eyes, but shalt not eat thereof.
corruption_summary: Malachi 3:10 has been detached from its covenant setting and made the proof text of prosperity preaching, in which giving is an investment technique and the windows open on demand.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity gospel rests more weight on this verse than on almost any other, and the handling is consistently dishonest in three ways. It is addressed to the covenant nation under the Mosaic law, in a specific moment of national robbery of the storehouse, and the blessing named is agricultural — the rebuking of the devourer and the fruitfulness of the vine. It is not a promise of financial return to individual donors, and still less to donors giving to the preacher who quotes it. The movement then inverts the verse's logic: Malachi's invitation to prove God is a rebuke to a people who were withholding, whereas the prosperity use turns it into a technique by which God's hand is moved, which makes the Almighty a mechanism and the giver the one in control.

The New Testament's own teaching on giving stands against the scheme without discouraging generosity, which is the balance to keep. Paul does promise that he who sows bountifully shall reap bountifully, but the reaping he names is grace sufficient for every good work, and he insists the giver purpose it in his heart, not grudgingly nor of necessity. Meanwhile the flood occurrences keep the figure honest. The same windows that pour out blessing poured out the waters that drowned the world, and the Samaritan lord who treated the phrase as a sarcasm about what God could not do was given exactly what he asked for and none of what he needed. The principle to recover is that heaven's openings are at God's discretion and not at man's disposal.

pos: n. phr. (the dew as a figure of blessing given from above, and of humiliation)
etymology: Hebrew tal ha-shamayim — tal, dew or night mist, and shamayim, the heavens; in Daniel the Aramaic tal shemayya. Dew in Palestine falls without rain and was indispensable to the summer crops.
biblical_def: The blessing Isaac intended for Esau and gave to Jacob begins with it: “Therefore God give thee of the dew of heaven, and the fatness of the earth, and plenty of corn and wine.” The order is theological as well as agricultural. Dew is named before the fatness of the earth because in that land the summer brings no rain at all, and the night dew carried the crops through the dry months; it falls silently, without thunder or cloud, and cannot be stored, gathered, or compelled. It is therefore Scripture's natural figure for a blessing that is purely given — daily, quiet, and wholly outside man's management. Isaac's word to Esau keeps the phrase but reverses its position: “thy dwelling shall be the fatness of the earth, and of the dew of heaven from above”, and the sequel shows how differently the two blessings ran. Daniel turns the figure to humiliation. Nebuchadnezzar is told that he shall be driven from men, shall eat grass as oxen, and “they shall wet thee with the dew of heaven, and seven times shall pass over thee, till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will.” The same dew that blesses a covenant son soaks a proud king sleeping in the open. In both cases it comes down from heaven unbidden, and in both it teaches the same lesson about who gives.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Dew, the moisture collected from the atmosphere and deposited on the surface of the earth in the night. The dew of heaven, Genesis 27:28, a figure of blessing silently given from above.
webster_full: Dew, the moisture deposited on the earth in the night season.
Hebrew tal, dew or night mist, indispensable to the summer crops.
God give thee of the dew of heaven, and the fatness of the earth, Genesis 27:28.

And Isaac his father answered and said unto him, Behold, thy dwelling shall be the fatness of the earth, and of the dew of heaven from above;
Dan 4:25

That they shall drive thee from men, and thy dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field, and they shall make thee to eat grass as oxen, and they shall wet thee with the dew of heaven, and seven times shall pass over thee, till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will.
And of Joseph he said, Blessed of the LORD be his land, for the precious things of heaven, for the dew, and for the deep that coucheth beneath,
corruption_summary: A figure for blessing that cannot be manufactured is read sentimentally, and the agricultural fact that gives it force — that the land lived on dew through a rainless summer — is unknown to most readers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. It suffers instead from a distance that flattens it. Readers in temperate countries with regular rainfall hear dew as a decorative word for morning freshness, and the blessing of Genesis 27:28 sounds like poetry rather than survival. In the land of the Bible the summer is rainless for months together, and the heavy night dew is what carried the vine and the grain through it. That is why the dew stands first in the blessing, ahead of the fatness of the earth: it is the daily, invisible, uncompellable supply without which there is no harvest to be fat.

Recovering the fact recovers the doctrine. Dew cannot be irrigated, stored, or bargained for; it descends or it does not. Scripture uses it accordingly for the kind of blessing that is wholly of gift — God's favour, His teaching dropping as the dew, the brethren dwelling in unity like the dew of Hermon. The counterpart in Daniel 4 keeps it from sentimentality: the same silent descent that nourishes a covenant household soaks a humbled king until he learns that the most High rules in the kingdom of men. The principle to recover is that the quiet provisions are the critical ones, that a man lives by mercies he never arranged, and that the right response to dew is not admiration of the scenery but thanks to the One who sends it down.

pos: n. phr. (the cities of the Jordan plain, chiefly Sodom and Gomorrah)
etymology: Hebrew are ha-kikkar — ir, a city, and kikkar, a round thing, hence the circuit or round plain of the Jordan. The Authorized Version uses the same English phrase in Deuteronomy for the cities of the Mishor, the tableland east of Jordan.
biblical_def: Lot's choice is told in these words: “Abram dwelled in the land of Canaan, and Lot dwelled in the cities of the plain, and pitched his tent toward Sodom.” The Hebrew kikkar means a round thing, and so the circuit of the Jordan, which Lot had just seen to be “well watered every where… even as the garden of the LORD”. The narrative traces a drift rather than a single decision: he dwells in the cities of the plain and pitches toward Sodom, and by the time the angels come he is sitting in its gate. The overthrow is recorded with the same phrase and with a striking clause attached: “And it came to pass, when God destroyed the cities of the plain, that God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow, when he overthrew the cities in the which Lot dwelt.” Lot is spared, and the stated reason is not his own merit but that God remembered Abraham, who had interceded. The destruction itself was total: “he overthrew those cities, and all the plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew upon the ground.” Readers should note that the Authorized Version uses the same phrase in a quite different geography in Deuteronomy 3:10, of the cities of the tableland in Og's kingdom, which has no connection with Sodom.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Plain, level land; an open field. The cities of the plain, Genesis 13:12, the cities of the round circuit of Jordan, chiefly Sodom and Gomorrah.
webster_full: Plain, level land; a flat or open country or field.
Hebrew kikkar, a round thing, hence the circuit or plain of Jordan.
Lot dwelled in the cities of the plain, Genesis 13:12.
God destroyed the cities of the plain, Genesis 19:29.
The same English phrase is used of the tableland cities, Deuteronomy 3:10.

And it came to pass, when God destroyed the cities of the plain, that God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow, when he overthrew the cities in the which Lot dwelt.
And he overthrew those cities, and all the plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew upon the ground.
Deu 3:10
All the cities of the plain, and all Gilead, and all Bashan, unto Salchah and Edrei, cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan.
corruption_summary: The sin of the cities is reassigned to inhospitality alone in order to clear the plain sense of the narrative, while the account's own warning about gradual settlement in them goes unread.
corruption_paragraphs: The revisionist reading, now standard in affirming scholarship, holds that the sin of Sodom was inhospitality and social injustice and had nothing to do with the sexual conduct the narrative describes. Ezekiel 16:49 is cited for it, and that verse does name pride, fulness of bread, and neglect of the poor — which the dictionary gladly receives, since Scripture names more sins in Sodom than one. But the very next verse adds that they “committed abomination before me”, and Jude writes that Sodom and Gomorrha gave themselves over to fornication and went after strange flesh, and Peter sets them forth as an example to the ungodly. A reading that must stop at Ezekiel 16:49 and decline Ezekiel 16:50, Jude 7, and 2 Peter 2:6 has not interpreted the text but selected from it.

The second failure is to read the chapter only as a judgment story and to miss the warning aimed at the believer. The narrative is careful about Lot's progress: he looked, he chose the well-watered circuit, he dwelt among the cities, he pitched toward Sodom, and at last he sat in its gate — and Peter says that righteous man vexed his soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds. He was not an enthusiast for the place; he was a believer who had settled in it by degrees and could not get his own family out. That he escaped at all is credited to God remembering Abraham's intercession. The principle to recover is that compromise is usually a drift and not a decision, and that the mercy which extracts a man from it is owed to God and not to his own good sense.

word: Land Flowing with Milk and Honey
pronunciation: LAND FLOH-ing with MILK and HUN-ee
pos: n. phr. (the standing description of the land promised to Israel)
etymology: Hebrew erets zabath chalab u-debash — zub, to flow or gush, with chalab, milk, and debash, honey or the thick syrup of dates. The participle is one of flowing, not of containing.
biblical_def: The phrase is the Pentateuch's standing description of Canaan, and it enters at the burning bush: “And I am come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians, and to bring them up out of that land unto a good land and a large, unto a land flowing with milk and honey.” It is repeated through the exodus narrative and into the prophets, where Jeremiah uses it of the oath God swore to the fathers. The pairing is pastoral and wild rather than agricultural. Milk is the yield of flocks and herds that need wide grazing; honey is gathered, not farmed. Together they describe a country that supports life abundantly without being first subdued — the opposite of Egypt, where Deuteronomy says the people sowed their seed and watered it with the foot, and the opposite also of the ground cursed in Genesis 3 which yields its increase only to sweat. The participle is flowing. The land is not described as holding milk and honey but as running with them, which is a figure of overflow. Two things must be held with it. The description is of a gift: Israel is given cities they did not build and vineyards they did not plant. And the gift is conditioned in its enjoyment, for the same books that promise the flowing land warn that the land itself will spue out its inhabitants for defilement.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Flowing, running as a liquid; abounding, overflowing. A land flowing with milk and honey, Exodus 3:8, the standing description of Canaan as a land of abundance given by God.
webster_full: Flowing, moving as a stream; abundant, copious, overflowing.
Hebrew zub, to flow, to gush out, to overflow.
Hebrew chalab, milk, the produce of flocks and herds.
Hebrew debash, honey; also the thick syrup of grapes or dates.
A good land and a large, a land flowing with milk and honey, Exodus 3:8.
scriptures: Exo 3:8

And I am come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians, and to bring them up out of that land unto a good land and a large, unto a land flowing with milk and honey; unto the place of the Canaanites, and the Hittites, and the Amorites, and the Perizzites, and the Hivites, and the Jebusites.
Exo 3:17

And I have said, I will bring you up out of the affliction of Egypt unto the land of the Canaanites, and the Hittites, and the Amorites, and the Perizzites, and the Hivites, and the Jebusites, unto a land flowing with milk and honey.
Exo 13:5

And it shall be when the LORD shall bring thee into the land of the Canaanites, and the Hittites, and the Amorites, and the Hivites, and the Jebusites, which he sware unto thy fathers to give thee, a land flowing with milk and honey, that thou shalt keep this service in this month.
Jer 11:5
That I may perform the oath which I have sworn unto your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey, as it is this day. Then answered I, and said, So be it, O LORD.
corruption_summary: The phrase is taken as a promise of material prosperity to the individual believer, and the covenant land given to a particular nation is converted into a guarantee of personal comfort.
corruption_paragraphs: The common misuse lifts the description out of the covenant with Israel and applies it to the Christian's circumstances, so that the land flowing with milk and honey becomes a figure for financial sufficiency, career advancement, or a season of ease that God owes the faithful. The exodus itself refutes the application. The generation to whom the promise was first spoken did not enter, and the writer to the Hebrews says plainly why: they could not enter in because of unbelief. The promise was real, the land was real, and most of those who heard it died in the wilderness. A reading that turns Exodus 3:8 into a guarantee of personal comfort has to ignore Numbers 14 and Hebrews 3 to do it.

The second corruption is a flattening in the other direction, in which the phrase is treated as mere poetic hyperbole for a pleasant country and the covenant content is dropped. Scripture gives it a far more exact weight. The land is described as flowing because it supports life without first having to be conquered by labour — a reversal of the curse on the ground — and it is given rather than earned, with cities Israel did not build. But possession and enjoyment are not the same thing, and Leviticus warns that the land will spue out its inhabitants for defilement, which is exactly what the exile proved. The principle to recover is that God's gifts are genuinely gifts and are genuinely held in covenant, and that the rest the land pictured is entered now by faith, which is the argument of Hebrews 4.

pos: n. phr. (the best and richest produce of a country)
etymology: English fat in its older sense of richness or the best part, rendering Hebrew cheleb, fat, which in the sacrificial law is the portion reserved to the LORD and so stands for the choicest of anything.
biblical_def: Pharaoh's invitation to Joseph's family supplies the phrase: “And take your father and your households, and come unto me: and I will give you the good of the land of Egypt, and ye shall eat the fat of the land.” The Hebrew cheleb is the fat of a beast, and its force here comes from the sacrificial law, where the fat is the portion burnt to the LORD and forbidden to the worshipper; it is the richest part, and therefore stands for the best of anything. To eat the fat of the land is to have the choicest produce of a country. Pharaoh adds to it, “regard not your stuff; for the good of all the land of Egypt is yours,” and the famine narrative makes the offer the more remarkable, since it comes in the middle of a worldwide dearth and is made to foreigners by a king whose storehouses Joseph had filled. The phrase is used elsewhere of what God gave Israel in Canaan: Nehemiah's confession recalls that they “took strong cities, and a fat land, and possessed houses full of all goods… so they did eat, and were filled, and became fat, and delighted themselves in thy great goodness.” That same prayer continues into the warning the phrase always carries in Scripture, for the sentence after is that they were disobedient and rebelled. Plenty is a gift and is also a test, and Nehemiah records both.

corruption_summary: The phrase has become a sneer at those who prosper, or a slogan for self-indulgence, where Scripture presents plenty as a gift received from God and a condition that proved perilous.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Its drift is one of tone. In ordinary English “living off the fat of the land” now carries a sneer, implying idleness at someone else's expense, and that is not its sense in Genesis 45. There it is a generous invitation extended to a famine-stricken household by the ruler of the country, in a famine God had foretold and provided against through the brother those same men had sold. The phrase in Scripture names plenty as given, and the giving is traced to God's providence running through a long and painful history.

Nehemiah 9 supplies the balance and should be read with it. Israel took a fat land, ate, were filled, and delighted themselves in God's great goodness — and the prayer immediately records that they then rebelled. Scripture is consistently clear-eyed about this: Deuteronomy warns that when the people have eaten and are full they must beware lest they forget the LORD, and Agur asks for neither poverty nor riches lest being full he deny God. None of this is a commendation of want for its own sake, which Scripture nowhere treats as holiness. The principle to recover is the discipline of thanksgiving in plenty: the fat of the land is a real good, really given, and the danger is never in the eating but in forgetting who set the table.

pos: n. phr. (the table in the holy place bearing the bread of the presence)
etymology: English shewbread, Tyndale's rendering of Hebrew lechem ha-panim, the bread of the face or presence; with table, Hebrew shulchan. The table is the article of furniture; the shewbread is what lay upon it.
biblical_def: The phrase occurs once in the Authorized Version, in the instructions for breaking camp: “And upon the table of shewbread they shall spread a cloth of blue, and put thereon the dishes, and the spoons, and the bowls, and covers to cover withal: and the continual bread shall be thereon.” The table stood in the holy place on the north side, over against the candlestick, and was made of shittim wood overlaid with gold, two cubits long, a cubit broad, and a cubit and a half high. Upon it were set twelve cakes of fine flour, “in two rows, six on a row, upon the pure table before the LORD,” renewed every sabbath, with the old loaves eaten by the priests in the holy place. The command concerning it is as plain as it is easy to pass over: “thou shalt set upon the table shewbread before me alway.” The Hebrew calls it the bread of the face — bread set before the presence of God. Its doctrine is covenantal rather than nutritional. The twelve cakes answer to the twelve tribes, so that the whole people stand continually represented before God in the holy place; alway and continual are the governing words; and the arrangement is one of fellowship, a table set and a meal shared in the house of God. The detail about the journey matters as well, for the table was carried covered but never emptied: the bread remained on it while Israel moved.

corruption_summary: The sanctuary furniture is treated as archaeological detail with no present claim, so that a table set continually before God — a picture of the people represented and fed in His presence — teaches nothing.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The neglect is the problem. Much modern reading treats the tabernacle chapters as inventory to be skimmed on the way to narrative, and a generation of Christians consequently cannot say what stood in the holy place or why. The loss is real, because the New Testament reasons from this furniture constantly and cannot be followed without it. Hebrews argues from the arrangement of the sanctuary; our Lord Himself appeals to the shewbread when the Pharisees charge His disciples with breaking the sabbath, reasoning from David eating the bread which was not lawful for him to eat.

The opposite error is over-reading, in which every dish and spoon is assigned a hidden meaning on no authority but the expositor's ingenuity, and the text becomes a code. Scripture's own emphases are the safe guide, and they are three: the bread is before the LORD, it is continual, and it is twelve. The people are represented, permanently, in the presence of God. That is a picture of intercession and of covenant memory, and it is answered in the New Testament by a High Priest who ever liveth to make intercession. The principle to recover is that the furniture preaches: a table set perpetually in God's house says that His people are kept before His face, and are fed there, and that neither the setting nor the feeding depends on their being in camp or on the march.

pos: n. phr. (a self-description of the beloved in the Song of Solomon)
etymology: Hebrew chabatstseleth ha-Sharon — chabatstseleth, a bulbous flower, probably the crocus or meadow-saffron rather than the rose of modern gardens; with Sharon, the coastal plain between Joppa and Carmel.
biblical_def: The phrase occurs once: “I am the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys.” Two points of accuracy should be noted at the outset. The Hebrew chabatstseleth denotes a bulbous flower and is most likely the crocus or meadow-saffron, not the rose of English gardens, which was unknown to the Hebrew of that period; the Authorized Version's rose is a translator's approximation for a bright wild flower. And Sharon is the broad coastal plain between Joppa and Carmel, a fertile and well-watered stretch celebrated for its pasture and its wild blossom. The force of the self-description is therefore its ordinariness. The speaker likens herself not to a rare garden specimen but to a common wild flower of the plain, one of thousands — and the beloved's reply takes up the figure and overturns it: “As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters.” What she offers as modesty he receives as singularity. The dictionary takes the Song as what it plainly is, a divinely-given poem of covenanted love between a man and his wife, and with the long Christian tradition also reads it typologically of Christ and His church. The traditional application of the title to Christ is an application, honourable and old, rather than a direct reading, since in the text itself the words are the bride's.

corruption_summary: The Song is either emptied of its plain sense as a poem of married love, or emptied of Christ by a reading that allows it nothing beyond the literal; and the title is routinely assigned to Christ as though the text said so.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite handlings have both damaged the Song. The older allegorising tradition was so embarrassed by a frank poem of married desire in the canon that it dissolved every physical detail into a spiritual cipher, with the result that what Scripture says about the goodness of covenanted love between husband and wife could not be heard at all. The modern reaction strips the book to a collection of ancient love lyrics with no further reference, and loses what the whole prophetic tradition does with marriage as the figure of God's covenant with His people — a figure Paul takes up explicitly in Ephesians 5 and calls a great mystery concerning Christ and the church. The dictionary holds both: the Song means what it says, and it means more.

A smaller point of honesty belongs here too. “Jesus is the Rose of Sharon” is a staple of hymnody and preaching, and as a devotional application it stands in a long and worthy line. But in Song of Solomon 2:1 the speaker is the bride, and a preacher who presents the verse as though Christ were there calling Himself the rose has told his people something the text does not say. The dictionary's rule on quotation applies to allusion as well: an application should be offered as an application. The principle to recover is that the Song honours married love as God's good gift and shadows the love of Christ for His church, and that neither of these is served by misreporting who is speaking.

pos: n. phr. (the anointing oil of joy, said of the Messiah)
etymology: Hebrew shemen sason — shemen, oil, and sason, joy or exultation; rendered in Greek elaion agalliaseōs. Oil was poured on the head at feasts as well as at the setting apart of kings and priests.
biblical_def: The phrase belongs to the forty-fifth psalm and to the citation of it in Hebrews. The psalmist addresses the king: “Thou lovest righteousness, and hatest wickedness: therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows.” Hebrews applies the verse directly to the Son: “Thou hast loved righteousness, and hated iniquity; therefore God, even thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows.” The force of the figure lies in the two uses of oil. It was poured on the head of a king or priest at his setting apart, and it was also used at feasts as a mark of welcome and rejoicing, as in the psalm where God anoints the head and the cup runs over. The oil of gladness holds both: a consecration which is also a joy. Two words govern the verse and both are easy to hurry past. Therefore grounds the anointing in a moral fact — this joy is given because righteousness was loved and wickedness hated, so the gladness is not detached from holiness but is its reward. And above thy fellows sets the Anointed apart in degree while implying that the fellows are anointed too. Isaiah's parallel promises the same to the mourners of Zion, though in the Authorized Version he writes it “the oil of joy for mourning”.

corruption_summary: Joy is reassigned to the emotions and made the measure of a believer's standing, severed from the righteousness the psalm names as the ground of the anointing.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern religious usage tends to treat joy as a feeling to be produced, managed, and displayed. Worship is arranged to generate it, its absence is diagnosed as a spiritual deficiency, and the Christian who cannot summon it is left to conclude that something has gone wrong between him and God. Psalm 45 locates the oil of gladness elsewhere. It is conferred, not worked up; it follows a therefore; and its ground is that righteousness was loved and wickedness hated. The therapeutic register, which treats emotional states as the thing to be optimised, cannot accommodate a joy that is given as a reward for holiness and is not in the recipient's gift.

The opposite failure is a Reformed temptation and must be named with the other. Where joy is regarded as suspect — enthusiasm, mere feeling, the province of less serious Christians — a dour piety results that Scripture does not commend. The oil of gladness is poured on the head of the Messiah Himself, who is the man of sorrows and acquainted with grief and is also anointed with joy above His fellows; the two are not rivals. Nehemiah says the joy of the LORD is the people's strength, and Paul commands rejoicing in the Lord alway. The principle to recover is the order: holiness first, and joy as its anointing, given from outside, resting on the Anointed and overflowing to His fellows.
